q1: SELECT beer, MAX(price) - MIN(price) AS price_gap, AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM serves WHERE beer IN (SELECT s.beer FROM serves AS s, frequents AS f WHERE s.bar = f.bar AND f.drinker LIKE 'B%' GROUP BY s.beer HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT s.bar) >= 2) GROUP BY beer ORDER BY beer
q2: WITH bars_frequented_by_b_drinkers AS (SELECT DISTINCT f.bar FROM frequents AS f JOIN drinker AS d ON f.drinker = d.name WHERE d.name LIKE 'B%'), beers_served_in_selected_bars AS (SELECT s.beer, s.bar, s.price FROM serves AS s JOIN bars_frequented_by_b_drinkers AS bfbb ON s.bar = bfbb.bar), beer_price_stats AS (SELECT beer, MAX(price) - MIN(price) AS price_gap, AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM beers_served_in_selected_bars GROUP BY beer) SELECT beer, price_gap, avg_price FROM beer_price_stats ORDER BY beer

explanation: Q1 filters beers served in at least 2 distinct bars frequented by B% drinkers, while Q2 includes all beers served in any such bar. This leads to Q1 excluding beers served in only one bar, while Q2 includes them.
counterexample_dsp: A beer (BeerA) served only in bar B1 (frequented by Bob), and BeerB served in both B1 and B2 (both frequented by B% drinkers). Q1 includes BeerB but not BeerA, while Q2 includes both.

That subquery selects beers from serves and frequents where the drinker starts with 'B', groups by beer, and has at least two distinct bars. So Q1 is getting beers that are served in at least two different bars frequented by B% drinkers, then calculates stats on those beers.

Now Q2 uses CTEs. The first CTE finds bars frequented by B% drinkers. Then, the second CTE gets beers served in those bars. The third CTE calculates the same stats as Q1. Then selects those results.

No. Because in Q2's beer_price_stats, it's grouping by beer, but the beers could be served in one bar only. Then, when grouping by beer in beer_price_stats, if a beer is served in only one bar (but that bar is frequented by a B% drinker), then the price gap would be zero (since max and min are same), and average is that price. However, in Q1, the subquery requires that the beer is served in at least two bars. So Q1's beer list is a subset of Q2's. Therefore, Q1 might exclude some beers that Q2 includes.

So the key difference is that Q1 requires that the beer is served in at least two different bars (from the B% drinkers' frequented bars), whereas Q2 includes all beers served in any of those bars, even if only in one bar. Therefore, if there's a beer served in exactly one of those bars, Q2 will include it but Q1 will not. That would be the case where the results differ.

So to create a counterexample, I need a beer that is served in exactly one bar (which is frequented by a B% drinker), and another beer that's served in two such bars. Then, Q1 would include the second beer but not the first. But Q2 would include both. So in that case, Q1's result would have the second beer's stats, while Q2 would have both.
